title: Adult Learning: Turn Experience into Practice
headline:
Good learning
starts with doing.
need: A trainer in a financial-services learning team has a dense procedure and a short session. Employees need practice making a quality decision, with enough guidance to apply the standard.
outcomes: Choose design moves that connect adult learners’ experience to a relevant task.
Revise a short training activity to include practice, feedback and evidence.

concepts.title: Start with a meaningful problem
concepts.body: Explain what the learner will be able to do and why it matters to the job. A concrete problem helps learners connect a session to their own work. Treat relevance as something to establish with the audience, not assume.

concepts.title: Use experience as material
concepts.body: Invite a brief example from prior work, then test the approach against the current task and standard. Experience can help learning, but old habits may also need revision. Avoid presenting one learner’s anecdote as universal evidence.

concepts.title: Offer useful choice and support
concepts.body: Give learners choices that still lead to the objective, such as selecting one of two practice contexts. Explain the goal and provide enough structure for novices. Self-direction does not mean leaving people without a model or feedback.

concepts.title: Practice, feedback, transfer
concepts.body: Let learners attempt the work, receive specific feedback and try again. Finish with a small workplace application and a way to inspect the result. Adult-learning principles are design guidance, not a claim that every adult has identical preferences.

example.title: Replace a 12-minute explanation
example.body: The old session describes a quality rubric for 12 minutes. Learners then rate their confidence. The job requires using that rubric to justify a quality decision.
steps: Open with a short anonymized quality decision.
Ask learners what evidence they would inspect.
Model one rating, then give a new case to rate.
Compare the rationale with the criteria and revise it.
Plan a real follow-up review with the quality coach.

practice.prompt: Which activity best uses prior experience without treating it as automatically correct?
options: Ask for an example, compare it with the current criteria, and revise the response
Skip the standard because everyone has experience
Ask learners to memorize everyone’s stories
practice.feedback: The activity respects experience while checking it against the work standard.

draft.prompt: Revise a lecture-only session on giving quality feedback. Include one relevant task, learner choice, feedback and a transfer check.
draft.label: Your activity redesign
draft.model: Choose one of two fictional coaching cases. Draft feedback tied to the quality criteria, compare it with a model, revise it, then ask a coach to review a future workplace example.
criteria: Uses experience or a meaningful choice
Names evidence for a later transfer check

options: Show the work problem and the task learners will practice
Start with a timer and no purpose
quiz.feedback: The work problem explains why the session matters.

quiz.prompt: A learner shares an outdated technique. What should the trainer do?
options: Accept it because experience always wins
Compare it respectfully with the current standard
quiz.feedback: Experience is useful material for analysis, not automatic proof.

options: Choose either of two cases requiring the same target skill
quiz.feedback: The context changes while the required performance stays aligned.

options: Good job, regardless of the response
Your rationale names a criterion; now connect it to specific case evidence
quiz.feedback: Specific feedback points to an actionable improvement.

options: A later work sample reviewed against the criteria
quiz.feedback: A later work sample tests use in context; satisfaction is different evidence.

jobaid: Name the job problem and target performance.
Connect prior experience to the current standard.
Offer bounded choice and sufficient support.
Include practice, feedback, revision and follow-up.
disclosure: Independent portfolio sample by Lorne Hopkins. Brand-inspired educational design; not official employer or vendor training. Scenarios and records are fictional.

creative.headline:
Good learning
starts with doing.
creative.role: You are an instructional designer helping trainers and SMEs turn a dense procedure into useful practice in a regulated financial-services environment.
creative.answer: Offer the requested demonstration, then guided practice and feedback. Experience in one role does not remove the need for support with a new task.

transcript:
Allow 4 minutes, including the decision and check. Fictional case: Harbor Service Desk is introducing a shared handoff form. A usable handoff contains an issue summary, the next owner, and the next action. Ten sampled handoffs contain four missing owners. The manager requests a presentation about the new process. Before building it, ask what people must do and what prevents them from doing it.

Andragogy, associated with Malcolm Knowles, offers assumptions concerning adults' need to know why, self-direction, experience, readiness, problem orientation, and motivation. These are useful questions for design, not guarantees about each adult. An experienced employee may be a novice with this tool; someone attending a mandatory session may need substantial guidance. Adult learning has multiple theoretical perspectives, and andragogy is not its single universal explanation. See the Penn State readings in Sources.

Worked example: replace “They are adults, so let them explore” with “Can they already locate the owner list and submit a practice handoff?” Observe the task, ask about obstacles, and offer a guided example when needed. In this sample, the instructional goal is a complete handoff. Fixing access to the owner list belongs in the implementation plan too.
